messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Publisher
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

He is 34, a Middle Eastern man who works in publishing, and when he first talks about what happened, he does so in the careful, edited way he describes manuscripts at work: as if precision might keep the worst parts contained. Before the trauma, he says, his life was busy but predictable. He spends long days reading submissions, meeting with authors, arguing over covers and print runs, then coming home late to his wife, who teases him for always bringing a stack of pages to bed. He likes order, deadlines, the quiet satisfaction of shaping other people’s stories into something coherent. What happened to his younger sister has made coherence feel false.

Two years ago, his sister is badly injured in a violent assault. He is not there when it happens. What he remembers first is the phone call—his mother’s voice sounding unlike itself, flattened by panic—and then the drive to the hospital, every red light feeling obscene. He still sees the emergency department in fragments: bright fluorescent glare, a security guard drinking coffee, blood on the cuff of a nurse’s scrub top, his brother-in-law pacing with both hands on his head. When he is finally allowed to see his sister, she is swollen, bruised, and barely conscious. He stands at her bedside and feels his mind separate from his body. He notices absurd details—the chipped blue polish on her thumbnail, the plastic pitcher of water no one can use—because looking directly at her face feels impossible.

In the weeks that follow, he becomes the competent one. He translates for relatives, updates family WhatsApp groups, talks to police, fills in forms, answers emails from work at 2 a.m. He tells himself there is no room for collapse. At the hospital he sits upright, carrying coffee and sandwiches, speaking in a calm voice. But at night he lies awake beside his wife, staring at the ceiling, replaying images he did not witness but cannot stop imagining. He sees his sister alone, afraid, calling for help. The scenes arrive fully formed and unwanted, with such force that his heart races as if he is inside them. Sometimes he gets up and checks the locks three or four times before he can attempt sleep again.

When his sister comes home, he expects relief. Instead, the world begins to feel dangerous in a permanent way. He startles at footsteps behind him and turns sharply when strangers come too close. On the subway he scans faces, exits, hands. If his wife is ten minutes late, he is already calling, then calling again. He insists on picking her up from places she used to go alone. He hears himself sounding controlling and hates it, but the alternative feels unbearable. He starts avoiding the neighborhood where the assault occurred, then entire parts of the city connected in his mind to hospitals, police stations, and late-night phone calls.

At work, the changes are quieter but more costly. Publishing has always depended on sustained attention, but now concentration slips through his hands. He reads the same paragraph repeatedly without retaining it. In meetings, if an author describes violence in a memoir or novel, his chest tightens and his mind drifts toward his sister’s injuries. He begins passing certain manuscripts to colleagues, saying they are “not the right fit,” though privately he knows he cannot bear the content. Deadlines that once energized him now provoke dread. He misses small errors he never would have missed before, then feels ashamed and stays late trying to compensate. The office, once a place of pleasure and identity, becomes another space where he is bracing himself.

His wife tells him he is present and absent at the same time. He sits beside her on the couch but jerks when she touches him unexpectedly. He is quicker to anger than he used to be, especially when he feels helpless: a slow cashier, a delayed train, an editor who uses the phrase “it’s out of our hands.” Sometimes he snaps and immediately regrets it. Sometimes he goes silent for hours. He does not tell many people what is happening inside him because he believes he should be grateful his sister survived. He compares himself to her and concludes he has no right to be struggling. That thought does not comfort him; it deepens his guilt.

He sleeps poorly. Some nights he dreams he is searching hospital corridors that keep lengthening, never reaching her room. Other nights he wakes drenched in sweat, certain the phone is ringing. Mornings are heavy, as if he has already lived a full day before getting out of bed. He has stopped seeing friends regularly. Noise exhausts him. Family gatherings, once warm and chaotic, now feel like performances in which everyone is trying not to say the wrong thing.

In session, what stands out is how much of his life is organized around preventing another catastrophe that he knows, rationally, he cannot fully prevent. He loves his sister fiercely; he loves his wife with the vigilance of someone who now understands how quickly ordinary life can rupture. He keeps telling himself that if he can stay alert enough, useful enough, careful enough, no one he loves will ever again become unreachable. Yet he is tired in a way that reaches beyond sleep, and even in safe rooms, with people he trusts, part of him remains on guard, listening for the phone call that will split his life in two again.
